## 1. Motivation and Context

Satellite imagery offers a powerful way to observe how places change and differ across cities and regions. It can capture information about buildings, roads, vegetation, water, and other features of the environment. However, turning these images into information that can easily be used for research or policy analysis has traditionally been difficult and time-consuming. Conventional approaches often require researchers to manually create specific measurements from imagery, such as vegetation indices, land-cover classifications, or texture measures. These methods are usually designed for one particular purpose and may not work well for other types of analysis. As a result, working with satellite imagery can require significant technical expertise and large amounts of preparation time.

The EMBED2SOCIAL data product aims to make this process much easier. It provides pre-computed satellite image embeddings for England and Wales, and equivalent statistical units in Scotland and Northern Ireland in 2024, aggregated to Lower-layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs). An embedding can be thought of as a numerical fingerprint of a place that captures important visual patterns from satellite imagery. Rather than storing the image itself, the embedding summarises important visual patterns in a form suitable for analysis. Each area is represented using a compact description of its surrounding environment. These embeddings are designed to act as a flexible, general-purpose representation of place that can support many different kinds of analysis.

This chapter demonstrates two key ways these embeddings can be used:

- **Exploring spatial patterns** – identifying groups of places that look similar without needing predefined categories.  
- **Predicting social outcomes** – using imagery-derived patterns to help estimate indicators such as deprivation levels.  

A key advantage of this approach is reusability. Instead of creating a new set of measurements for every individual project, the same embedding representation can support many different applications. This makes spatial analysis faster, more scalable, and more accessible to researchers and policymakers without specialist expertise in remote sensing or machine learning. More broadly, these approaches can help researchers and policymakers better understand patterns of inequality, urban change, environmental conditions, and neighbourhood characteristics.

## 2. The EMBED2SOCIAL Data Product
The EMBED2SOCIAL data product provides ready-to-use satellite image embeddings for neighbourhoods across England and Wales, alongside equivalent statistical units in Scotland and Northern Ireland. The purpose of the dataset is to make information contained within satellite imagery more accessible for social, spatial, and urban analysis.

Rather than working directly with large collections of satellite images, users can work with a compact set of numerical variables that summarise the visual characteristics of each area. These variables can be integrated into standard statistical, mapping, and machine-learning workflows in the same way as more familiar socioeconomic or environmental datasets.

#### 2.1. What Does the Dataset Contain?
For each neighbourhood, the dataset provides a set of 64 embedding variables:

A00_mean, A01_mean, ..., A63_mean

Together, these variables provide a numerical description of the surrounding environment derived from satellite imagery. They capture information related to the overall visual character of a place, including patterns associated with buildings, roads, vegetation, open space, and land-use structure.

The variables should be interpreted collectively rather than individually. Unlike traditional remote sensing products, such as vegetation indices or land-cover classifications, each embedding dimension does not correspond to a specific physical feature. Instead, the 64 variables work together to represent the overall appearance of a neighbourhood.

#### 2.2. Dataset Characteristics
| Attribute                     | Description                                                             |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Source imagery                | Google satellite imagery (2024)                                         |
| Spatial unit                  | Lower-layer Super Output Areas (LSOAs) and equivalent statistical units |
| Geographic coverage           | England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland                          |
| Number of embedding variables | 64                                                                      |
| Aggregation method            | Mean embedding value within each statistical unit                       |
| Output formats                | GeoPackage (.gpkg) and GeoJSON                                          |

#### 2.3. Thinking About Embeddings as Place Descriptions

A useful way to think about the embedding variables is as a numerical description of place.

Neighbourhoods with similar visual characteristics tend to have similar embedding values, while visually different neighbourhoods tend to have different embedding values. This allows the same dataset to be used for a wide range of analytical tasks without creating new image-derived variables for each project.

For example, the embeddings can support:
- Identifying neighbourhoods with similar visual characteristics
- Exploring patterns of urban form and land use
- Clustering places into groups with comparable environments
- Modelling socioeconomic outcomes
- Mapping deprivation and inequality
- Supporting environmental and public health research


Because the embeddings provide a general-purpose representation of place, the same dataset can be reused across multiple applications. This reusability is one of the main advantages of the EMBED2SOCIAL data product and forms the basis of the examples presented in the remainder of this chapter.

```{python}
from IPython.display import Image, display
```

### 3.1. Input Data
Our input dataset is the annual (2017-2024) Google Satellite Embedding:

- It is not simply satellite images that we used to see in the navigators.
- Embeddings represent a combination of multiple remote sensing datasets, produced by a comprehensive computer vision model.
- The model learns complex visual patterns and converts them into a 64-dimensional embedding space.

### 3.2. Embedding Extraction
To organise the input embeddings, we:

- Access terabytes of embedding data stored in Google Earth Engine (2017-2024).
- Select data in the area and period of interest.
- Efficiently store 858 embedding tiles for further processing.

### 3.3. Spatial Aggregation
Each embedding dimension is aggregated to the level of statistical units - LSOAs in England and Wales, and equivalent geographies in Scotland and Northern Ireland. Each dimension matters for different aspects of geospatial analysis, so all 64 dimensions are retained in the final dataset.

### 3.4. Final Data Product

The final output consists of eight tables covering the period from 2017 to 2024, each containing the same set of spatial units. Also, for every statistical unit, the dataset includes 64 aggregated embedding values.

This provides a comprehensive representation of each neighbourhood that can be readily integrated into geospatial, statistical, and machine learning workflows.

## 5. Use case 1: Semantic Similarity Analysis

### 5.1. Why Semantic Similarity Matters

Traditional spatial analysis often relies on geographic proximity. However, places that are geographically distant can share similar physical characteristics, while neighbouring areas can appear very different.

Satellite image embeddings allow us to move beyond geographic distance and instead measure similarity in terms of visual and environmental characteristics captured from imagery.

In this context, embeddings can be viewed as coordinates within a semantic space. Areas that are close together in this space share similar visual patterns, while areas further apart appear more different.

This allows researchers to identify neighbourhoods that "look alike" even when they are located in different parts of a city or country.

### 5.2. Extracting Embedding Representations

The EMBED2SOCIAL dataset contains 64 embedding dimensions (A00_mean to A63_mean) for each LSOA. Together, these dimensions provide a compact numerical representation of the visual characteristics of a neighbourhood derived from satellite imagery.

Rather than describing a single feature, such as vegetation cover or building density, the embedding dimensions collectively capture a broad range of information related to the built and natural environment, including patterns associated with buildings, roads, green space, land use, and urban structure.

For the semantic similarity analysis, we only require the embedding variables. We therefore extract the 64 embedding dimensions from the full dataset and store them separately for subsequent analysis.

```{python}
# Extract embedding dimensions only
embeddings = gdf.loc[:, "A00_mean":"A63_mean"]
```

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/}
# Display dimensions of embedding matrix
embeddings.shape
```

These embedding vectors can be viewed as coordinates in a high-dimensional semantic space, where neighbourhoods with similar visual characteristics tend to occupy nearby positions.

### 5.3. Finding Similar Neighbourhoods
Once each neighbourhood has been represented by its embedding, we can identify places that look similar based on satellite imagery.

Rather than comparing every neighbourhood with every other neighbourhood, we use a nearest-neighbours algorithm. This method efficiently searches the embedding space and finds the most similar areas for each location.

Here, we use the NearestNeighbors function from the scikit-learn library to identify the five most similar neighbourhoods for every LSOA.

The nearest-neighbour algorithm identifies the most visually similar neighbourhoods for every LSOA based on embedding distance.

```{python}
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

# Define nearest-neighbour model
nn = NearestNeighbors(
    n_neighbors=6,   # includes the area itself
    metric="cosine"
)

# Fit model to embedding vectors
nn.fit(embeddings)

# Retrieve nearest neighbours
dist, neigh = nn.kneighbors(embeddings)
```

The model searches for neighbourhoods with the most similar embedding values. The output includes:

- dist – stores that distances between each area and its nearest neighbours.
- neigh – the corresponding neighbouring areas.

### 5.4. Creating a Semantic Neighbour Table

The nearest-neighbour algorithm returns the positions of similar areas within the dataset rather than their actual LSOA codes. To make the results easier to interpret, we convert these positional indices back into the corresponding geographic identifiers. This creates a lookup table that lists the most semantically similar neighbourhoods for every LSOA in the dataset.

The first neighbour returned by the algorithm is always the area itself (distance = 0), so this is removed. The remaining neighbours represent the most visually similar locations according to the embedding representation derived from satellite imagery.

```{python}
neigh_codes = (
    pd.DataFrame(
        neigh[:,1:],
        index=gdf["data_zone_code"]
    )
    .map(lambda i: gdf["data_zone_code"][i])
)
```

Once the semantic neighbour table has been created, we can query any LSOA and retrieve its closest neighbours in embedding space. For example, the following code identifies the five most similar neighbourhoods to LSOA E01035718.

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/, height: 238}
neigh_codes.loc["E01035718"]
```

The output is a list of LSOA codes corresponding to neighbourhoods whose satellite imagery exhibits similar visual characteristics. These similarities may reflect common patterns in urban form, green-space structure, building density, road networks, or other environmental features captured by the embeddings.

### 5.5. Visualising Semantic Neighbours

Having identified the nearest semantic neighbours, we can now examine whether these areas genuinely appear similar in satellite imagery. By visualising the reference neighbourhood alongside one of its nearest neighbours, we can assess how effectively the embedding representation captures meaningful characteristics of place. With this, we're good to go to explore semantic similarity.

#### Example: Hyde Park Neighbourhood

The following example selects the LSOA containing Hyde Park and identifies its most semantically similar neighbourhoods using the embedding representation.

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/, height: 572}
gdf.query(
    'data_zone_code=="E01035718"'
).geometry.explore()
```

```{python}
m2 = (

    )
)

# Side-by-side display
display(HTML(
    "<div style='display:flex'>" +
    f"<div style='width:50%'>{m1._repr_html_()}</div>" +
    f"<div style='width:50%'>{m2._repr_html_()}</div></div>"
))
```

## 6. Use Case 2: Predicting Socioeconomic Outcomes

### 6.1. From Exploration to Prediction

The previous example demonstrated how satellite image embeddings can be used to explore geographic space and identify neighbourhoods with similar visual characteristics. In this section, we explore a different application: predictive modelling.

Predictive modelling uses existing observations to learn relationships between variables and then applies those relationships to estimate outcomes for new locations.

The aim here is not to build the most sophisticated machine learning model possible. Instead, the objective is to demonstrate how satellite image embeddings can be integrated into a standard analytical workflow and to assess whether they contain useful information about socioeconomic conditions.

Specifically, we investigate whether information contained within satellite image embeddings can help predict neighbourhood deprivation levels.

This case demonstrates:

* How embeddings can be combined with socioeconomic data.
* How predictive models can be developed using different information sources.
* Whether embeddings improve predictive performance.
* How predictive results can be interpreted spatially.

### 6.2. Data Used for Prediction

Two datasets are used in this analysis.

### Embedding Dataset

The first dataset is the EMBED2SOCIAL dataset which was introduced earlier in this chapter.

For the embedding dataset, each LSOA contains:

* geographic identifiers;
* geometry;
* 64 embedding variables (`A00_mean`–`A63_mean`).

Together, these variables provide a compact numerical description of the visual characteristics of a neighbourhood derived from satellite imagery.

### Socioeconomic Dataset

The second dataset contains socioeconomic variables linked to each LSOA.

This dataset includes:

| Variable                              | Description                                     |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| IMD_decile                            | Index of Multiple Deprivation (target variable) |
| Percent no qualifications 16 and over | Educational attainment                          |
| Percent bad and very bad health       | Health status                                   |
| Population density per km             | Population density                              |
| Percent lone family household         | Household structure                             |

The Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) decile is used as the prediction target.

### 6.3. Loading and Preparing the Data

We have introduced the EMBED2SOCIAL dataset previously in this chapter. Here we load the socioeconomic data into the working environment. This dataset is provided as a CSV file and includes the IMD deciles, along with additional variables identified in the literature as influencing deprivation. IMD deciles group areas into ten categories, where lower deciles indicate higher levels of deprivation and higher deciles indicate lower levels of deprivation.

```{python}

# Load socioeconomic data

df = pd.read_csv("datasets/Socioeconomic.csv")
```

Preview the data:

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/, height: 238}
df.head()
```

This dataset contains the deprivation labels and additional socioeconomic variables used in the predictive modelling analysis.

### 6.4. Combine Socioeconomic and Embedding Data

To perform prediction, the socioeconomic data is linked to the embedding dataset using the common LSOA identifier *LSOA21CD*, allowing the embedding variables to be combined with the socioeconomic variables for each LSOA.

```{python}
# Join embedding data with socioeconomic data
# Merge on the common LSOA identifier to combine both datasets
gdf2 = gdf.merge(
    df,
    on="LSOA21CD",
    how="left"
)
```

The merge operation creates a single dataset, and we inspect the merged dataset to confirm that embedding and socioeconomic variables have been successfully merged.

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/, height: 576}
gdf2.head()
```

The resulting dataset now contains:

* embedding variables;
* socioeconomic variables;
* deprivation indicators;
* spatial geometry.

This combined dataset forms the basis of the predictive modelling exercise.

### 6.5. Explore the Spatial Distribution of Deprivation

Before building a predictive model, it is useful to visualise the variable we wish to predict. In this regard, visualising the IMD data on a map helps reveal the spatial distribution of deprivation across London and makes patterns easier to interpret than tabular form.

The following function creates an interactive web map showing the spatial distribution of a selected variable.

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/, height: 572}
# -----------------------------------------
# Interactive map of IMD deciles
# -----------------------------------------

# Add reference points (Name, latitude, longitude)
# These provide spatial context and help orient the map
pois = """
"Westminster", 51.4975, -0.1357
"City of London", 51.5155, -0.0922
"Canary Wharf", 51.5054, -0.0235
"King's Cross", 51.5308, -0.1238
"Heathrow Airport", 51.4700, -0.4543
"WE ARE HERE :)", 51.4962, -0.1298
"""

# Ensure the GeoDataFrame has a coordinate reference system (CRS)
# Use EPSG:4326 only if the coordinates are already longitude/latitude
if gdf2.crs is None:
    gdf2 = gdf2.set_crs(epsg=4326)

# Create interactive map
# Visualises IMD deciles across LSOAs with tooltips and optional basemaps
m = make_webmap_general(
    focus_gdf=gdf2,
    focus_col="IMD_decile",
    focus_name="LSOA IMD Deciles",
    focus_tooltip_cols=("LSOA21CD", "LSOA21NM", "IMD_decile"),
    focus_categorical=True,
    focus_legend=True,
    focus_cmap="YlOrRd_r",
    focus_style_kwds={
        "fillOpacity": 0.6,
        "weight": 0.2,
        "color": "black",
    },
    context_gdf=None,
    pois=pois,
    fit_to="focus",
    zoom_start=10,
)

# Display map
m
```

**Function Explanation**

The function:

```python
make_webmap_general()
```

creates an interactive web map.

Key inputs include:

| Parameter          | Purpose                    |
| ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| focus_gdf          | Dataset to map             |
| focus_col          | Variable displayed         |
| focus_tooltip_cols | Information shown on hover |
| focus_legend       | Display map legend         |
| focus_cmap         | Colour scheme              |

This helps to understand the spatial distribution of deprivation before modelling begins.

### 6.6. Building a Baseline Model to Predict IMD Using Only Socioeconomic Variables

The first model uses only socioeconomic variables.

This provides a baseline against which embedding-based models can be compared.

The model includes:

* educational attainment;
* health status;
* population density;
* household structure.

A Random Forest classifier is used, which is an ensemble of decision trees. It can capture non-linear relationships and interactions between variables without requiring assumptions such as proportional odds used in ordinal logistic regression.

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/}
# Train a classifier to predict IMD decile using selected socioeconomic predictors
results_socio = run_rf_classifier(
    data=gdf2,
    y_col="IMD_decile",
    x_cols=[
        "Percent no qualifications 16 and over",
        "Percent bad and very band health",
        "Population density per km",
        "Percent lone family household",
    ],
)
```

**Function Explanation**

The function:

```python
run_rf_classifier()
```

builds and evaluates a Random Forest classification model.

Important parameters include:

| Parameter    | Description                     |
| ------------ | ------------------------------- |
| data         | Input dataset                   |
| y_col        | Variable being predicted        |
| x_cols       | Predictor variables             |
| test_size    | Proportion reserved for testing |
| n_estimators | Number of trees                 |
| random_state | Reproducibility setting         |

This model answers:

> How accurately can deprivation be predicted using socioeconomic information alone.

### 6.7. Predicting IMD Using Embedding Variables Only

Here, we investigate whether satellite image embeddings alone contain useful information about deprivation.

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/}
# -----------------------------------------
# Run Random Forest model (embedding features only)
# -----------------------------------------

# Define embedding feature columns (A00_mean to A63_mean)
feature_cols = [f"A{i:02d}_mean" for i in range(64)]

# Train classifier to predict IMD decile using embedding features
results = run_rf_classifier(
    data=gdf2,
    y_col="IMD_decile",      # Target variable (deprivation decile)
    x_cols=feature_cols,     # Embedding predictors
    test_size=0.2,           # Proportion of data used for testing
    random_state=42,         # Ensures reproducibility
    n_estimators=500,        # Number of trees in the forest
    class_weight="balanced", # Handle class imbalance
)
```

This model uses only the embedding representation derived from satellite imagery.

No socioeconomic variables are included.

The purpose is to evaluate whether visual characteristics captured by the imagery are associated with neighbourhood deprivation.

### 6.8. Predicting IMD Using Combined Information

Embeddings are not intended to replace conventional datasets.

Instead, they often provide complementary information.

To test this, we combine socioeconomic variables and embeddings in a single model.

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/}
# -----------------------------------------
# Run Random Forest model (embeddings + socioeconomic variables)
# -----------------------------------------

# Define predictor variables
# Combine embedding features with selected socioeconomic indicators
feature_cols = (
    [f"A{i:02d}_mean" for i in range(64)] +
    [
        "Percent no qualifications 16 and over",
        "Percent bad and very band health",
        "Population density per km",
        "Percent lone family household",
    ]
)

# Train classifier to predict IMD decile
results = run_rf_classifier(
    data=gdf2,
    y_col="IMD_decile",      # Target variable (deprivation decile)
    x_cols=feature_cols,     # Combined predictors
    test_size=0.2,           # Proportion used for testing
    random_state=42,         # Reproducibility
    n_estimators=500,        # Number of trees
    class_weight="balanced", # Handle class imbalance
)
```

This model examines whether the two information sources complement each other and they together produce better predictions.

### 6.9. Comparing Model Performance

Three models have now been created:

| Model   | Predictors                           |
| ------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Model 1 | Socioeconomic variables only         |
| Model 2 | Embeddings only                      |
| Model 3 | Socioeconomic variables + embeddings |

Their predictive results are shown below.

| Model              | Accuracy | Mean Absolute Error |
| ------------------ | -------- | ------------------- |
| Socioeconomic only | 0.276    | 1.42                |
| Embeddings only    | 0.197    | 1.94                |
| Combined model     | 0.338    | 1.11                |

#### **Interpretation**

Several important findings emerge:

**1**. Embeddings alone are able to predict deprivation better than random chance, indicating that satellite imagery contains meaningful socioeconomic information.

**2**. Traditional socioeconomic variables remain strong predictors.

**3**. The best performance is achieved when embeddings and socioeconomic variables are combined.

This suggests that embeddings capture aspects of neighbourhood context that are not fully represented by conventional datasets.

### 6.11. Visual Analytics and  Spatial Interpretation - side by side

Model accuracy statistics help evaluate predictive performance, but they do not explain where relationships occur geographically.

Mapping variables alongside deprivation helps users interpret model results spatially.

To this end, this chapter concludes with a series of side-by-side map comparisons.

#### **Quantile Classification**

```{python}

# -----------------------------------------

show_two_maps_side_by_side(
    gdf2,
    left_var="IMD_decile",                        # Deprivation (target variable)
    right_var="Percent no qualifications 16 and over",  # Socioeconomic predictor
    tooltip_cols=("LSOA21CD", "LSOA21NM"),        # Information shown on hover
    scheme="quantile",                            # Classification method
    k=10,                                         # Number of classes
)
```

Quantile classification places an equal number of neighbourhoods into each class.

This is useful for comparing relative rankings across areas.

#### **Equal Interval Classification**

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/, height: 292}

# Compare two variables using equal intervals
# -----------------------------------------

# Visualise IMD deciles alongside a socioeconomic variable

show_two_maps_side_by_side(
    gdf2,
    left_var="IMD_decile",                         # Deprivation (target variable)
    right_var="Percent no qualifications 16 and over",  # Socioeconomic predictor
    scheme="equal",                                # Equal-interval classification

```

Equal interval classification divides the data range into classes of equal width.

This highlights absolute differences between neighbourhoods.

#### **Natural Breaks**

```{python}
#| colab: {base_uri: https://localhost:8080/, height: 292}
# -----------------------------------------
# Compare two variables using natural breaks
# -----------------------------------------

# Visualise IMD deciles alongside a socioeconomic variable
# Values are grouped using natural breaks (Jenks), which highlight
# inherent groupings in the data
show_two_maps_side_by_side(
    gdf2,
    left_var="IMD_decile",                         # Deprivation (target variable)
    right_var="Percent no qualifications 16 and over",  # Socioeconomic predictor
    scheme="natural",                              # Natural breaks (Jenks)
    k=10,                                          # Number of classes
    tooltip_cols=("LSOA21NM",),                    # Information shown on hover
)
```

Natural breaks classification identifies clusters that occur naturally within the data.

This often provides a more realistic representation when values are unevenly distributed.

### 6.12 Key Takeaways

This predictive modelling example demonstrates how a single embedding dataset can support predictive modelling without requiring additional image processing or feature engineering.

The analysis shows that:

* satellite imagery contains information related to socioeconomic conditions;
* embeddings can be used directly in standard machine-learning workflows;
* embeddings complement traditional socioeconomic datasets;
* combining information sources often produces the strongest predictions;
* mapping remains essential for interpreting model outputs and understanding spatial patterns.

More broadly, this example illustrates the central idea behind EMBED2SOCIAL: a reusable representation of place that can support multiple analytical tasks, from exploratory analysis to predictive modelling, using the same underlying embedding dataset.

## 7. Opportunities and Limitations

The examples presented in this chapter illustrate how satellite image embeddings can support both exploratory and predictive forms of spatial analysis. By transforming imagery into compact numerical representations, embeddings provide a flexible way to describe places that can be integrated into standard analytical workflows.

### 7.1. Opportunities

One of the most important advantages of embeddings is their reusability. Traditional remote sensing approaches often require researchers to design task-specific variables, such as vegetation indices, land-cover maps, or manually engineered image features. In contrast, a single embedding representation can support many different applications without requiring new feature extraction for each task.

As demonstrated in this chapter, the same embeddings were first used to identify semantically similar neighbourhoods and then reused to predict socioeconomic outcomes. This ability to support multiple analytical tasks from a common representation reduces the amount of data preparation required and makes imagery more accessible to users without specialist expertise in remote sensing.

Embeddings also provide opportunities for:

- Exploring neighbourhood similarity beyond geographic proximity;
- Identifying patterns of urban form and land use;
- Supporting predictive modelling of social, environmental, and economic indicators;
- Integrating Earth observation data into conventional statistical workflows;
- Enabling large-scale analysis across cities, regions, and countries.

Because embeddings can be generated consistently across extensive geographic areas, they offer a scalable framework for analysing spatial patterns in a way that is difficult to achieve using traditional manually derived indicators.

### 7.2. Limitations

Despite their potential, embeddings should not be viewed as a complete replacement for conventional spatial and socioeconomic data.

A key limitation is interpretability. Individual embedding dimensions do not correspond directly to observable physical characteristics such as vegetation cover, building density, or road length. Instead, information is distributed across many dimensions, making it difficult to assign a simple meaning to any single variable.

The predictive examples presented in this chapter also highlight an important consideration: embeddings capture patterns and associations rather than causal relationships. A strong predictive relationship between imagery and deprivation does not necessarily imply that visual characteristics cause deprivation. Rather, the imagery may reflect environmental and urban conditions that are associated with broader socioeconomic processes.

The quality of embedding-based analysis is also influenced by the quality of the underlying imagery and the embedding model used to generate the representations. Different image sources, resolutions, acquisition dates, or model architectures may lead to different embedding characteristics.

Finally, the usefulness of embeddings depends on the analytical question being addressed. In some applications they may provide substantial additional information, while in others traditional variables may already explain most of the variation of interest.

For these reasons, embeddings are best viewed as complementary sources of information that can enrich existing analytical approaches rather than replace them.

## 8. Conclusions

This chapter has demonstrated how satellite image embeddings can be used as a general-purpose representation of geographic space.

Unlike traditional remote sensing products that are often designed for a single application, embeddings provide a flexible description of place that can be reused across multiple analytical tasks. Using the EMBED2SOCIAL data product, we illustrated this principle through two complementary examples.

First, semantic similarity analysis showed how embeddings can be used to explore neighbourhoods that share similar visual characteristics, regardless of their geographic location. By representing places within a high-dimensional semantic space, embeddings enable researchers to identify meaningful spatial relationships that may not be apparent from physical distance alone.

Second, predictive modelling demonstrated how the same embeddings can be combined with conventional socioeconomic indicators to estimate deprivation levels. The results showed that embeddings contain useful information about neighbourhood context and can improve predictive performance when used alongside traditional datasets.

Taken together, these examples highlight the central value of embedding-based representations: a single set of image-derived features can support both exploratory and predictive analysis without the need to repeatedly engineer new variables from imagery.

As Earth observation archives continue to expand and foundation models become increasingly common, embedding-based data products are likely to play an increasingly important role in spatial data science. They provide a practical bridge between large-scale imagery resources and applied research in urban studies, social science, environmental monitoring, public health, and policy analysis.

The EMBED2SOCIAL data product represents one example of this emerging paradigm, demonstrating how satellite imagery can be transformed into reusable spatial information that supports a wide range of analytical questions. Rather than replacing existing data sources, embeddings provide an additional layer of evidence that can help researchers better understand the social, environmental, and spatial characteristics of places.
